newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania wheat exports seen affected by low quality.
newsitem.headline: Romania wheat exports seen affected by low quality.

text.p: Romania has harvested more than 20 percent of its wheat crop and figures show crop yields are good but wheat exports might be harmed by recent rains which affected the crop's quality, an official said on Friday.

"The quality of the wheat harvested over the past week is low. Our wheat might not be in very big demand for export this year," Vasile Duta, general manager of the National Agency for Agricultural Products (ANPA), told Reuters.
Agriculture Minister Dinu Gavrilescu said harvesting had been completed so far on 23 percent from the 2.38 million hectares under wheat.
Data showed an average yield of 3,155 kilograms per hectare, higher than the ministry's initial estimates of 2,968.

"However, we expect to get in the end an average yield close to the 2,968 level as the wheat harvested so far comes from the southern areas, usually more productive than the rest of the country," Dinulescu said.
The ministry expects a total wheat crop of 7.07 million tonnes in 1997, almost double the level last year.
Duta said heavy rains in recent days had affected the quality of the wheat crop, with gluten contents dropping to 74 percent, from 83 percent, and increased humidity in the grains.
"These figures are pretty low and very close to standard-wheat quality. They might raise some concerns over good prospects for milling wheat exports," he said.
Last month, the ministry put wheat exports at 2.4 million tonnes on the assumption of a bumper crop this year.
"At this stage, it is impossible to confirm this figure or to give a new estimate," Duta said.
He said limited handling capacities in the Black Sea port of Constanta, Danube River ports and on the country's railways added to the problem.
Data supplied by ANPA, a state-run body monitoring the grain market, showed Romania could handle some 230,000 tonnes of wheat per month.

The data showed the silo in the Black Sea port of Constanta could handle up to 150,000 tonnes a month, the Danube ports of Braila, Galati and Tulcea some 40,000 tonnes while a floating crane in the port of Agigea, near Constanta, could discharge from barges and load into ships around 40,000 tonnes a month.
A plan to build a new 100,000-tonne silo in Constanta is currently under consideration but work on the project is not expected to start for two years.
